title: Controlled Substance Schedule Overview
subtopic: Federal schedules and Massachusetts Schedule VI
learning_objectives: Separate federal controlled-substance status from Massachusetts scheduling consequences.
Identify the legal consequence that actually controls instead of reasoning from a schedule label alone.

orientation.text: Controlled-substance classification is a lookup rather than a judgement about how a drug behaves. Federal law collects the schedules established by section 202 of the Controlled Substances Act into 21 CFR Part 1308, one section per schedule: 1308.11 for Schedule I, 1308.12 for Schedule II, 1308.13 for Schedule III, 1308.14 for Schedule IV and 1308.15 for Schedule V. Each of those sections opens with the same sentence -- the schedule 'shall consist of the drugs and other substances, by whatever official name, common or usual name, chemical name, or brand name designated, listed in this section' -- and most of them go on to state that each drug or substance has been assigned the Controlled Substances Code Number set forth opposite it. Membership therefore turns on what the words of a listing reach. Some listings name a substance; others describe a class, as 21 CFR 1308.12(b)(1) reaches 'opium and opiate, and any salt, compound, derivative, or preparation of opium or opiate' before naming the substances it excludes. A class term carries the definition the law gives it rather than its clinical sense: under 21 CFR 1300.01(a) a term Part 1300 does not define takes the meaning set out in 21 U.S.C. 802, and 21 U.S.C. 802(18) defines 'opiate' by an addiction-forming or addiction-sustaining liability similar to morphine. That is why a drug-specific question has to be answered from the exact schedule provision, read with its defined terms and its own exclusions, rather than from a drug's pharmacologic family or an undifferentiated reference to Part 1308.

In Massachusetts the lookup runs through those same federal lists. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 2(a) directs the Commissioner to establish by regulation five schedules incorporating the five federal schedules, and a sixth schedule which shall include all prescription drugs not included in the first five. 105 CMR 700.002 carries that out: 700.002(A) provides that Massachusetts Schedule I consists of the drugs and other substances, by whatever official name, common or usual name, chemical name, or brand name designated, listed in 21 CFR 1308.11, and (B) through (E) repeat that formula for 1308.12 through 1308.15 in turn. As the regulation is currently written, then, Massachusetts Schedules I through V hold exactly what the federal sections list, and a drug's federal listing settles its Massachusetts schedule without a second scheduling decision to look up. The statute still leaves Massachusetts free to act on its own: under s. 2(a1/2) the Commissioner may delete or reschedule substances by regulation, and must issue a regulation controlling a newly federally controlled substance in a corresponding schedule not more than 30 days after the federal notice or statute; and under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 2A the Commissioner may, on the findings that section requires and by an order taking effect after a 14-day notice period, place a substance in Schedule I on a temporary basis, for up to one year. So the lookup is always to the Massachusetts schedules in force, and it is 105 CMR 700.002 in its present form that makes Schedules I through V the federal lists.

105 CMR 700.002(F) provides that Schedule VI consists of all prescription drugs which are not included in any other schedule established by the Commissioner. It is a residual category defined by exclusion, so nothing about a drug's own pharmacology puts it there; a prescription drug reaches Schedule VI precisely because the federal lists that Massachusetts Schedules I through V incorporate do not reach it. What follows next is the point candidates most often get backwards. Schedule VI is a schedule of controlled substances: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 defines a controlled substance as a drug, substance, controlled substance analogue or immediate precursor in any schedule or class referred to in that chapter, and s. 2(a) makes the sixth schedule one of those schedules, so every Schedule VI drug is a controlled substance under Massachusetts law. What it lacks is federal status: because Massachusetts Schedules I through V currently adopt 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15 whole, a drug that reaches Schedule VI is one no federal schedule lists, and Schedule VI status does not by itself make a drug federally controlled. The accurate picture is a Massachusetts controlled-substance schedule with no federal counterpart, not a set of drugs sitting outside controlled-substance law. A Massachusetts rule written for controlled substances reaches Schedule VI unless the rule carves Schedule VI out -- M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(f), for instance, forbids refilling any controlled-substance prescription unless the original provides for refilling and specifies the number of refills -- while a rule written for Schedules II through V does not reach Schedule VI by those words.

Monitoring is the consequence most often attached to the wrong label, in both directions. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(a)(1) directs the Department to maintain an electronic system monitoring the prescribing and dispensing of all schedule II to V, inclusive, controlled substances and certain additional drugs, and defines additional drugs as substances the Department determines to carry a bona fide potential for abuse; 105 CMR 700.001 defines an Additional Drug as a controlled substance in Schedule VI so determined. The reporting regulation follows the same line: 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) applies to every pharmacy registered with the Commissioner that dispenses, pursuant to a prescription, a controlled substance in Schedules II through V or one the Department has classified as an additional drug, and to an out-of-state pharmacy delivering such a substance to a person in Massachusetts, while 700.012(A)(2) takes dispensing pursuant to a medication order to a hospital inpatient outside the regulation altogether. A Schedule VI drug becomes reportable when the Commissioner determines under 105 CMR 700.012(C)(8) that it is an additional drug, weighing factors such as a risk of addiction, known recreational use, known regular diversion for misuse or a known contribution to overdose, and notifies all dispensers that they must begin to report it. Two conclusions follow: a drug can be reportable without appearing in any federal schedule, and a Schedule VI drug is not reportable merely because it is in Schedule VI.

Two disciplines follow from that architecture. The first is to finish the classification properly: the schedule paragraphs in 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15 are typically prefaced 'Unless specifically excepted or unless listed in another schedule', and a number of the listings turn on quantity and formulation rather than on the active ingredient alone, so the thing being classified is the product in hand and not the molecule's reputation. The second is to treat the schedule as a premise. It identifies which body of dispensing, refill, transfer, partial-fill, record and reporting rules must now be opened, and those rules supply the answers. A rule may attach its consequence to a schedule directly, but it is the rule that states the consequence, and the same label can carry different consequences in the two sovereigns. A candidate who stops at the label has done the lookup and skipped the rule.

worked_examples.scenario: A prescriber sends an ordinary prescription for a maintenance medicine that appears nowhere in 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15. A student asks which Massachusetts schedule it sits in, whether that makes it a controlled substance at all, and whether the pharmacy therefore owes the record and reporting duties that attach to controlled substances.
steps: Start with Massachusetts Schedules I through V. 105 CMR 700.002(A) through (E) define each of them as the drugs listed in the matching federal section, so as the regulation is currently written a drug absent from 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15 is absent from Massachusetts Schedules I through V as well.

Ask the question 105 CMR 700.002(F) then puts: is it a prescription drug? If it is, it falls into Schedule VI, which consists of all prescription drugs not included in any other schedule established by the Commissioner.

Settle its status in each sovereign before reaching for any duty. It is a controlled substance in Massachusetts, because M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 defines a controlled substance by reference to the chapter's schedules and s. 2(a) makes the sixth schedule one of them. It is not federally controlled, because no section of 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15 lists it.

Sort the duties accordingly. No federal controlled-substance duty arises, and a Massachusetts rule written for Schedules II through V does not reach the drug by those words. A Massachusetts rule written for controlled substances does reach it unless that rule carves Schedule VI out, which is why the refill condition in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(f) applies to it.

Take reporting separately, because it turns on a determination rather than on the schedule. The dispensing is reportable only if the Commissioner has determined the drug to be an additional drug under 105 CMR 700.012(C)(8) and notified dispensers; absent that, M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(a)(1) and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) reach Schedules II through V rather than this drug.
worked_examples.resolution: It is a Massachusetts Schedule VI controlled substance that no federal schedule lists. No federal controlled-substance duty and no Schedule II through V duty follows from that, but the Massachusetts rules written for controlled substances do apply to it unless they exclude Schedule VI, and it becomes reportable if the Department designates it an additional drug. The scenario invites two opposite errors: importing federal or Schedule II through V duties that no listing imposes, and treating Schedule VI as though it sat outside controlled-substance law.

worked_examples.scenario: Two liquid preparations of the same narcotic active ingredient arrive on one order. The first contains 1.5 grams of codeine per 100 milliliters together with an active nonnarcotic ingredient in a recognized therapeutic amount. The second contains 150 milligrams of codeine per 100 milliliters together with a non-narcotic active medicinal ingredient, present both in a recognized therapeutic amount and in sufficient proportion to confer on the preparation valuable medicinal qualities other than those the narcotic possesses alone. A colleague files both as Schedule II on the ground that codeine is a Schedule II drug.
steps: Test the colleague's premise. 21 CFR 1308.12(b)(1) does place codeine in Schedule II, but that paragraph is prefaced 'Unless specifically excepted or unless listed in another schedule', so the listing yields to a narrower placement.

Read the first preparation against 21 CFR 1308.13(e)(1)(ii), which covers not more than 1.8 grams of codeine per 100 milliliters with one or more active, nonnarcotic ingredients in recognized therapeutic amounts. At 1.5 grams per 100 milliliters the preparation is within that listing, so it is Schedule III.

Read the second against 21 CFR 1308.15(c)(1), which covers not more than 200 milligrams of codeine per 100 milliliters or per 100 grams, in a preparation including one or more non-narcotic active medicinal ingredients in sufficient proportion to confer on it valuable medicinal qualities other than those possessed by narcotic drugs alone. At 150 milligrams per 100 milliliters, with its non-narcotic ingredient in that proportion, it is within the listing; without that proportion the Schedule V paragraph would not reach it.

Resolve the overlap the second preparation creates. Its strength and its nonnarcotic ingredient also answer the words of the Schedule III listing, and the preface decides between them: 21 CFR 1308.13(e) applies only 'unless specifically excepted or unless listed in another schedule', and the Schedule V paragraph lists it, so the narrower placement takes it.
Carry both answers into Massachusetts without a second lookup, because 105 CMR 700.002(C) and (E) consist of exactly the drugs listed in 21 CFR 1308.13 and 21 CFR 1308.15.
worked_examples.resolution: The two preparations are Schedule III and Schedule V respectively, and neither is Schedule II. The error is classifying the active ingredient instead of the product, which is exactly what the quantity thresholds, the conditions each listing attaches to its non-narcotic ingredients, and the 'unless listed in another schedule' preface exist to prevent.

worked_examples.scenario: A technician proposes a shortcut for the controlled-substance shelf: anything acting at an opioid receptor is a Schedule II narcotic and should be stored and recorded as one. You are asked to confirm the shortcut before the shelf is rearranged.
steps: Go to the provision rather than the class name. 21 CFR 1308.12(b)(1) places opium and opiate, and any salt, compound, derivative or preparation of opium or opiate, in Schedule II.

Read its class term as the law defines it. 'Opiate' is not defined in 21 CFR Part 1300, so under 21 CFR 1300.01(a) it takes the meaning in 21 U.S.C. 802(18): a drug or other substance having an addiction-forming or addiction-sustaining liability similar to morphine, or capable of conversion into one. The listing's test is that liability, not activity at a receptor.

Read the rest of that sentence. It excludes a list of substances by name -- among them naloxone, naltrexone, nalmefene, nalbuphine, naloxegol, naldemedine, samidorphan, dextrorphan and apomorphine, together with their respective salts -- so the Schedule II opiate listing does not reach them at all.

Note precisely what that decides. It settles that paragraph (b)(1) is not the source of any control over those substances. Whether one of them is controlled by some other listing is a separate question, answered by reading the other paragraphs of 21 CFR 1308.12 as well as 1308.11 and 1308.13 through 1308.15, because an exclusion from paragraph (b)(1) does not by its own terms reach another paragraph, and the opiates paragraph at 1308.12(c) carries exceptions of its own.

Apply the same reading to Massachusetts without a fresh lookup, because 105 CMR 700.002(A) through (E) consist of the drugs listed in those same federal sections, and a prescription drug they do not reach falls to Schedule VI under 105 CMR 700.002(F), where it is a Massachusetts controlled substance but not a federally controlled one.
worked_examples.resolution: The shortcut is wrong and cannot be repaired. A listing reaches what its own words describe, read with the definitions the law gives them: the class term 'opiate' is defined by addiction-forming or addiction-sustaining liability rather than by receptor activity, and several opioid-receptor drugs are named out of the Schedule II listing. The error is treating a pharmacologic class as though it were a classification, the same mistake as treating 'stimulant' as a schedule.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: 105 CMR 700.002(F) provides that Schedule VI consists of ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: all prescription drugs which are not included in any other schedule established by the Commissioner.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The federal schedules occupy 21 CFR ______ through ______, one section per schedule; Massachusetts states all of its schedules at 105 CMR ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: 1308.11 through 1308.15; 105 CMR 700.002(A) through (F). Five federal schedules, six Massachusetts ones.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Why, as 105 CMR 700.002 is currently written, does a drug's Massachusetts Schedule II status follow from its federal listing, and what could change that?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Because 105 CMR 700.002(B) defines Massachusetts Schedule II as the drugs and other substances listed in 21 CFR 1308.12, adopting the federal list rather than restating it, and 700.002(A) and (C) through (E) do the same for the other four schedules. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 2(a1/2) still lets the Commissioner delete or reschedule substances by regulation, and s. 2A lets the Commissioner place a substance in Schedule I temporarily by order.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: in Massachusetts, a prescription drug that appears in no federal schedule is not a controlled substance.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. It is in Schedule VI under 105 CMR 700.002(F), and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 defines a controlled substance as a drug, substance, controlled substance analogue or immediate precursor in any schedule or class referred to in the chapter, which s. 2(a) makes include the sixth schedule. It is a Massachusetts controlled substance that no federal schedule lists.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a drug in Massachusetts Schedule VI is federally controlled.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. Massachusetts Schedules I through V currently consist of the drugs listed in 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15, so a drug that reaches Schedule VI is one those sections do not list, and Schedule VI status does not itself establish federal controlled status.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What makes a Schedule VI drug reportable to the prescription monitoring program?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The Commissioner's determination under 105 CMR 700.012(C)(8) that it is an additional drug because it carries a bona fide potential for abuse, followed by notice to all dispensers that they must begin to report it. Schedule VI status alone does not.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: if a drug is reportable to the prescription monitoring program it must be federally scheduled.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(a)(1) reaches all schedule II to V controlled substances and additional drugs, and 105 CMR 700.001 defines an additional drug as a controlled substance in Schedule VI the Department has determined to carry a bona fide potential for abuse, which no federal schedule lists. 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) states the pharmacy's duty in the same terms, and 700.012(A)(2) excludes dispensing pursuant to a medication order to a hospital inpatient. Reportability also does not alter a drug's federal schedule.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The schedule paragraphs of 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15 typically open with the same qualifier. Quote it, and say what work it does.
retrieval_prompts.answer: 'Unless specifically excepted or unless listed in another schedule.' It makes each listing yield to a specific exception and to a narrower placement elsewhere, which is how one active ingredient can sit in more than one schedule at different quantities.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A listing reaches 'opium and opiate, and any salt, compound, derivative, or preparation of opium or opiate'. Where does the meaning of 'opiate' come from?
retrieval_prompts.answer: From 21 U.S.C. 802(18), by way of 21 CFR 1300.01(a), which gives any term not defined in Part 1300 the definition in section 102 of the Act: a drug or other substance having an addiction-forming or addiction-sustaining liability similar to morphine, or capable of conversion into one.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: You have established that a drug is a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription drug and appears on no federal list. What have you still not answered?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Whatever the question actually asked. Classification is only the premise; the refill, transfer, partial-fill, record or reporting consequence comes from the rule governing that act -- and because the drug is a Massachusetts controlled substance, that includes any Massachusetts rule written for controlled substances which does not carve Schedule VI out.

quick_review.text: Federal controlled-substance schedules are defined in 21 CFR Part 1308 and drug-specific classification requires the applicable schedule provision, read with its defined terms and exclusions.

105 CMR 700.002(A) through (E) currently make Massachusetts Schedules I through V the drugs listed in 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15, while M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 2(a1/2) and s. 2A let Massachusetts reschedule by regulation or place a substance in Schedule I temporarily by order.
Massachusetts Schedule VI captures prescription drugs not otherwise placed in Massachusetts Schedules I through V.

Every Massachusetts Schedule VI drug is a controlled substance under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 and s. 2(a), so a Massachusetts rule written for controlled substances, such as the refill condition in s. 23(f), reaches it unless the rule carves Schedule VI out.
A Massachusetts Schedule VI label does not by itself establish federal controlled status.

Dispensing a Schedule II through V controlled substance on a prescription is reportable to the prescription monitoring program under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(a)(1) and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1); dispensing a Schedule VI drug is reportable once the Commissioner has determined it to be an additional drug under 105 CMR 700.012(C)(8) and notified dispensers.

decision_logic.condition: A question asks whether a named drug is federally controlled.
decision_logic.action: Identify the drug's exact federal schedule provision and read the listing's words with their defined terms, its exclusions and its quantity and formulation limits before applying any federal consequence.

decision_logic.condition: A prescription drug is not in Massachusetts Schedules I through V.
decision_logic.action: Treat it as a Massachusetts Schedule VI controlled substance under 105 CMR 700.002(F), then apply the separate rule governing the requested act, including any Massachusetts rule written for controlled substances that does not carve Schedule VI out.

decision_logic.condition: A question asks whether a dispensing must be reported to the prescription monitoring program.
decision_logic.action: Ask whether the drug is in Schedules II through V or has been determined by the Commissioner to be an additional drug; if neither, the monitoring-program reporting duty does not reach it, and if the dispensing is pursuant to a medication order to a hospital inpatient, 105 CMR 700.012(A)(2) puts it outside the regulation.

ma_vs_federal.text: A Massachusetts Schedule VI drug is a controlled substance under Massachusetts law and is not federally controlled: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 and s. 2(a) make the sixth schedule one of the chapter's schedules, while 105 CMR 700.002(A) through (E) currently adopt 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15, so a drug that reaches Schedule VI is one no federal schedule lists.

Reportability to the Massachusetts prescription monitoring program turns on M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A and 105 CMR 700.012 rather than on federal scheduling: a Schedule VI drug the Department has determined to be an additional drug is reportable although no federal schedule lists it, and that determination does not change the drug's federal status.
Federal scheduling and Massachusetts Schedule VI answer different classification questions; neither label alone supplies every dispensing, transfer, or reporting consequence.

exceptions.text: A drug-specific or act-specific rule may add a narrower consequence, so classification is the start of the analysis rather than the final answer.
A Massachusetts rule written for controlled substances reaches Schedule VI unless it carves Schedule VI out; one written for Schedules II through V does not reach Schedule VI by those words.

105 CMR 700.012(A)(2) takes dispensing pursuant to a medication order to a hospital inpatient outside the monitoring-program reporting regulation, whatever the schedule, and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(b) states the same exclusion at statute level.

Massachusetts Schedules I through V match the federal lists because 105 CMR 700.002(A) through (E) currently adopt them; M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 2(a1/2) allows deletion or rescheduling by regulation and s. 2A a temporary Schedule I placement by order, so the current Massachusetts text is what governs.

role_duties.duty: Confirm the controlling federal and Massachusetts classification, reading the listing's own words, before applying an act-specific rule.

Report dispensing of Schedule II through V controlled substances and of any drug the Commissioner has determined to be an additional drug to the prescription monitoring program, except dispensing pursuant to a medication order to a hospital inpatient.

common_traps.text: Treating every Massachusetts Schedule VI drug as federally controlled is incorrect.

Treating a Massachusetts Schedule VI drug as though it were outside controlled-substance law is equally incorrect: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 makes a drug in any of the chapter's schedules, the sixth included, a controlled substance, which is why s. 23(f)'s refill condition reaches it.
Treating the schedule label as a complete answer to refill, transfer, or reporting questions skips the operative rule.

Assuming a monitored drug must be federally scheduled, or that a Schedule VI drug can never be monitored, overlooks the additional-drug determination under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(a)(1) and 105 CMR 700.012(C)(8).
Reading a class term such as 'opiate' as a pharmacologic label rather than as the defined term 21 U.S.C. 802(18) supplies leads to classification by receptor activity instead of by the listing.
